coaching.title: Today's Run
coaching.message: This is race day. You race the Julian Alps 50K today at Kranjska Gora. Don't run this morning. Eat a solid breakfast (80–100g carbs, moderate protein, low fiber), stay hydrated, and keep moving gently to stay loose—10 minutes of easy walking if anything. Your last three runs averaged 132 bpm, which is controlled; your resting HR is 65 bpm and recovery score is 70/100, meaning you're adequately fresh. Trust the taper. The sparse aid stations on this alpine course demand discipline with pacing on the climbs and aggressive fueling early (gels/sports drink every 45 minutes up). You've done the work over 34 weeks.

coaching.title: Fuel Right
coaching.message: Breakfast 2–3 hours before start: oatmeal or toast with honey and a banana, plus 500 ml of sports drink or water. This gives you glycogen topped off without gut stress. On the course, you'll face 2,500m of vert with sparse aid; pack your own calories (6–8 gels minimum, one energy bar, electrolyte tabs). Drink to thirst but don't underestimate alpine sun and exertion—aim for 500–750 ml per hour depending on terrain. Post-race, consume 1.2g carbs per kg body weight within 30 minutes and protein within 2 hours to begin recovery.

coaching.title: Recovery
coaching.message: Sleep was solid at 7.81 hours with 84.3% efficiency—you're not sleep-deprived going in. After the race, prioritize immediate fueling, then ice bath or cold immersion if available (15 minutes to reduce inflammation from alpine descents). Tonight, aim for 8–9 hours and don't stress if you're wired post-effort. Tomorrow (Saturday), do nothing; Sunday, an easy 4–5 mile shakeout at Z2 (130 bpm) to flush legs. Resting HR will tick up 2–3 bpm for 48 hours post-50K—that's normal.

coaching.title: Mental Edge
coaching.message: You've trained through constant travel as a Corp Dev exec and never missed a session. The alpine terrain will be steep and exposed; manage it by running the tangent lines tight, breaking the race into 3 aid-station segments, and remembering that your aerobic base (weeks 1–15) and peak vert work (weeks 16–19) prepared you for this exact stimulus. When legs feel heavy on climbs—mile 20–30—that's normal, not failure. Descents are where executives who train smart gain time; lock your quads, trust your footwork, and go. You've got this.
